chapters.title: Chapter 3: Completing and Stress-Testing the DCF

lessons.title: Sensitivity Tables and Scenario Analysis for Your DCF

children.text: Two lessons ago, Kaveri Ridge Cement's DCF produced a value of ₹248.6 per share, against a market price of ₹300. That number looks precise. It is not. It rests on a 15.4% margin, an 11.5% WACC, a 5% perpetual growth rate and a lawyer's 50:50 guess about a royalty dispute. Change any of them and the answer moves. The honest output of a DCF is not a number but a map: which assumptions drive the value, how far, and what has to be true for the market price to make sense.

body.text: A DCF value is only as reliable as its most sensitive assumption. Sensitivity tables show you which inputs matter. Scenarios show you what happens when the whole story changes. Together they turn a single false-precision number into a decision.

children.text: Step 1: Find the Inputs That Matter
test. Move each input across a reasonable range, one at a time, with everything else held at the base case. Rank them by how far value swings.

markDefs.definition: Changing a single input between a reasonable low and high value while holding all others at the base case, to see how much the valuation moves. Often displayed as a tornado chart.

body.title: Kaveri Ridge value per share when each input moves (base case ₹248.6)

data.label: Revenue growth (-2 pts / +2 pts a year)

body.caption: One-at-a-time sensitivity, ranked by swing (₹ per share)

cells: Revenue growth (-2 pts / +2 pts a year)

children.text: For Kaveri Ridge, WACC and EBIT margin dominate. A single percentage point of ebit margin moves value by more than a two percentage point change in revenue growth every year. That tells you where to spend your research time: understanding the cement price cycle and the company's cost position matters far more than refining the growth forecast to a decimal place.

body.text: The ranking changes by business. For a cement company, margin and discount rate usually dominate. For a young consumer or technology company, revenue growth and the length of the high-growth period often matter most. For a bank, it is return on equity and credit costs. Run the tornado before you run anything else.

children.text: The two inputs you cannot pin down, and that interact, belong in a two-way table. For almost every DCF, WACC and perpetual growth are the first pair, because together they drive terminal value. A tick marks values at or above the ₹300 market price.

body.caption: Kaveri Ridge value per share: WACC (rows) × perpetual growth (columns)

children.text: Only 4 of the 25 combinations reach ₹300, and all of them require a WACC at the low end of the range together with higher perpetual growth. For the current price to be justified on these two inputs alone, you would need to believe Kaveri Ridge is less risky and will grow faster forever than the base case assumes.
The second table pairs the two operating drivers: EBIT margin and revenue growth, with each year's growth shifted up or down by two percentage points.

body.caption: Kaveri Ridge value per share: EBIT margin (rows) × revenue growth shift (columns)

body.label: Break-even: what justifies ₹300?
body.value: EBIT margin of 17.4%, or a WACC of 10.7%
body.context: Holding everything else at the base case. Kaveri Ridge's current margin is 15.4%. Ask whether a sustained margin of 17.4% is realistic for a mid-sized cement company across a full cycle. The next lesson turns this question into a method: the reverse DCF.

body.text: Beware narrow ranges. A table that varies WACC from 11.4% to 11.6% and growth from 4.9% to 5.1% will show a reassuringly tight band of values, and tell you nothing. Use ranges that reflect genuine uncertainty. The discount rate alone can move a full percentage point in a year: when the RBI raised the repo rate by a cumulative 250 basis points between May 2022 and February 2023, long-term government bond yields rose sharply too.

children.text: For Kaveri Ridge, a one percentage point rise in WACC, from 11.5% to 12.5%, cuts value from ₹248.6 to ₹203.0 per share, a fall of 18%, with no change at all in the business.
Step 3: Scenarios That Tell a Complete Story
Sensitivity tables change inputs mechanically. Real outcomes do not work that way. When the cement cycle turns, prices, volumes and returns fall together.
groups assumptions into coherent stories and values each one.

markDefs.definition: Valuing a company under a small number of internally consistent stories about the future, such as bear, base and bull cases, each with its own set of assumptions, and weighting them by probability.

cells: New capacity floods southern markets; a price war compresses margins and the royalty dispute is lost
Steady demand, stable pricing, expansion ramps up as planned
Strong infrastructure spending and industry consolidation lift prices and utilisation
Royalty dispute: probability of paying ₹900 crore

body.title: Kaveri Ridge: scenario values vs market price (₹ per share)

body.caption: ₹ per share, probability-weighted across the three scenarios

children.text: The scenarios reshape the conclusion. The bull case sits well above the market price, so the ₹300 price is not absurd: it is roughly the market paying for a story partway between base and bull. But the bear case is severe, and the probability-weighted value of ₹243.6 is still below ₹300. An investor buying at ₹300 is making a bet that the bull case is more likely than 25%. That is a clear, testable statement, which is exactly what a valuation should give you.

body.text: Notice that the scenarios are not symmetric. The bear case falls further below the base than the bull case rises above it, because a price war, a lost legal case and returns falling to WACC arrive together. Real risks are often lopsided. A plus-or-minus 10% band around the base case hides that.

columns.label: Good practice
points: Each scenario is a coherent story with linked assumptions
The bear case reflects a real, named risk such as new capacity or a lost dispute
Probabilities are set before seeing the resulting values
Ranges reflect history, such as past margin troughs and peaks
Scenarios are revisited when the facts change

columns.label: Box-ticking
points: Bull and bear are just the base case plus or minus 10%
The bear case is "slightly slower growth"
Probabilities are adjusted until the weighted value supports the conclusion
Ranges are chosen to look reasonable, not to reflect what has happened
Scenarios are built once and never updated

body.title: Probability-weighted value
body.prompt: Your DCF for an auto ancillary company gives ₹180 per share in a bear case (30% probability), ₹250 in a base case (50%) and ₹360 in a bull case (20%). What is the probability-weighted value per share, in ₹?

body.title: Reading a two-way table
body.question: In the Kaveri Ridge WACC × growth table, values reach the ₹300 market price only at low WACC and high perpetual growth. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The stock is certainly overvalued and will fall to ₹249
The DCF is wrong because it does not match the market price
The market price implies lower risk and faster perpetual growth than the base case, which you should test against evidence
You should lower WACC until the DCF matches the market price
body.explanation: A sensitivity table does not tell you the price will move. It tells you what you would have to believe for the price to be justified. The right next step is to ask whether a lower WACC and higher perpetual growth are supported by the company's risk and competitive position. Adjusting inputs to match the price defeats the purpose of valuing the company independently.

body.title: Which input first?
body.textWithBlank: Before building scenarios, run a one-at-a-time sensitivity test to find which ___ move the valuation the most.
body.explanation: Ranking inputs by their impact on value tells you which assumptions deserve the most research and which belong in your two-way tables and scenarios.

body.title: The reassuring sensitivity table
body.scenario: Karthik, a portfolio manager at a Chennai-based PMS, reviews a junior analyst's DCF of a listed specialty chemicals company. The model shows a value of ₹1,840 per share against a market price of ₹1,500. The sensitivity table varies WACC from 11.8% to 12.2% and perpetual growth from 5.8% to 6.2%, and every cell is between ₹1,790 and ₹1,900. The analyst writes: "Valuation is robust. Upside of at least 19% in all scenarios." The company's EBITDA margin has ranged from 14% to 27% over the last ten years and is currently 26%. The model holds it at 26% forever.
body.prompt: What should Karthik tell the analyst?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The ranges are far too narrow. A 0.4 percentage point range for WACC and perpetual growth reflects none of the real uncertainty. Use at least plus or minus one percentage point for WACC and a perpetual growth range of about 4% to 6%.
2. The table tests the wrong inputs. For a specialty chemicals business whose margin has swung between 14% and 27%, margin is almost certainly the most important driver. It is not in the table at all.
3. The margin assumption sits near a cyclical peak. Holding 26% forever when the ten-year range is 14% to 27% values the best part of the cycle as permanent. The base case should use something closer to the long-term average, with 26% only in a bull case.
4. "All scenarios" is misleading. There are no scenarios, only small mechanical variations. The analyst should build a bear case with margins falling toward 14 to 16% as Chinese competition or raw material costs return, a base case near the average, and a bull case near current levels, each with linked growth and reinvestment.
5. Run a tornado first. Ranking inputs by impact will show where the valuation is fragile, and the conclusion will very likely change from "robust upside" to a much wider and possibly negative range.

body.title: Build a two-way sensitivity table in Excel
steps: Make sure your DCF calculates value per share in a single cell that depends on separate input cells for WACC and perpetual growth.
In an empty area, enter WACC values down a column and growth values across a row, leaving the top-left corner cell empty.
In that top-left corner cell, link to your value-per-share cell, for example =B45.
Select the whole block, including the row and column of values.
Go to Data, then What-If Analysis, then Data Table. Set the row input cell to your growth input and the column input cell to your WACC input.
Format the results, and highlight cells above and below the current market price.
Repeat for margin against revenue growth, then build bear, base and bull cases as separate, complete sets of inputs.

points: A DCF value is a range, not a point. Present it with sensitivity tables and scenarios.
Start with a one-at-a-time sensitivity to rank inputs by impact, then focus research on the few that dominate.
Use two-way tables for interacting inputs such as WACC and perpetual growth, or margin and revenue growth, with genuinely wide ranges.
Break-even analysis asks what you must believe to justify the market price, which is often more useful than the base case value.
Scenarios should be coherent stories with linked assumptions and probabilities set before seeing the results.
Real risks are often asymmetric. A severe, plausible bear case can matter more than a modest gap between base value and market price.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Kaveri Ridge Cement Ltd, the other companies described and the individuals named are fictional, and all figures, scenarios and probabilities are illustrative. The reference to RBI rate changes is approximate. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
